analysis.investment_thesis: CCL Products is a legitimate growth story — India's largest instant coffee exporter with a 14.3% nine-year revenue CAGR — but the Magic Formula metrics disappoint: earnings yield is ~3.4% (EBIT ₹555 Cr / EV ₹16,227 Cr) and ROCE of 13.1% sits well below my thresholds. The debt-funded capacity expansion is destroying free cash flow, and the business is not earning high enough returns on the capital it is deploying.
key_strengths: World's largest private-label instant coffee exporter with a nine-year revenue CAGR of 14.3%, scaling from ₹932 Cr to ₹3,106 Cr with operating income growing in lockstep
Strong promoter ownership (46.1%) and institutional backing (DII 21.4%) signal high conviction from informed capital
Continental brand (domestic) provides consumer-facing pricing power alongside B2B scale advantages in export markets
key_risks: Earnings yield of ~3.4% is far below the 6% floor — the market is pricing in a pristine growth trajectory with zero margin of safety
Debt has ballooned from ₹655 Cr (FY22) to ₹1,813 Cr (FY25), driving finance costs from ₹16 Cr to ₹113 Cr (29.5% CAGR) — rapidly eroding interest cover
Free cash flow has been negative for three consecutive years (FY23: -₹159 Cr, FY24: -₹458 Cr, FY25: -₹128 Cr) — the business is consuming capital, not generating it
red_flags: ROCE of 13.1% is below my minimum — the company is expanding aggressively into capacity that earns sub-threshold returns on incremental investment
Capex of ₹418 Cr in FY25 on ₹290 Cr OCF means the company burned ₹128 Cr more than it generated — not the hallmark of a Magic Formula business
Finance cost trajectory (29.5% CAGR vs 10.9% net profit CAGR) is a structural squeeze: if coffee prices soften, debt servicing will bite hard
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Magic Formula calculation: EV = ₹14,511 Cr market cap + ₹1,813 Cr debt − ₹97 Cr cash = ₹16,227 Cr. EBIT (Operating Income FY25) = ₹555 Cr. Earnings yield = 3.42% — fails badly. ROCE = 13.1% — also below my 20% threshold. Both legs of the formula are red; I cannot recommend the stock on value grounds regardless of the narrative quality.

The underlying business — spray-dried, agglomerated, and freeze-dried instant coffee for global private labels — is genuinely interesting and has scale. The problem is that management is reinvesting at a 13% ROIC using debt at high cost, creating a situation where growth destroys rather than creates value. Until the capacity investment cycle concludes, ROIC normalises above 20%, and earnings yield clears 6% (which would require the stock to trade at roughly half its current price), CCL fails my screen.
